question: The EU is the world’s second-largest importer of hunting trophies, yet the overwhelming majority of trophies entering the EU, i.e. most species listed in Annex B to Council Regulation (EC) No 338/97, do not require import permits, despite the fact that permits are required when the same species are imported for other purposes.

As import permits are the only mechanism for assessing whether trade is detrimental to species survival, the Scientific Review Group cannot conduct non-detriment assessments for most hunting trophy imports, limiting a key safeguard of the EU wildlife trade control system.

The need for greater scrutiny of trophy imports is recognised in the EU Action Plan against Wildlife Trafficking1 and Parliament’s resolution on CITES CoP202, which calls for import permits to be extended to all Annex B trophies. In this context: 1.
What is the scientific rationale for excluding most Annex B hunting trophies from import permit requirements?
How does the Commission ensure effective scrutiny where permits are not required, and is it open to extending permit requirements to all Annex B trophies? If not, why not?
What are the Commission’s plans for assessing additional species, beyond those under discussion, for possible inclusion in Annex XIII to Commission Regulation (EC) No 865/2006?

Commission communication of 9 November 2022 entitled ‘Revision of the EU action plan against wildlife trafficking’ (COM(2022)0581). 2 European Parliament resolution of 23 October 2025 on the EU strategic objectives for the 20th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), to be held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, from 24 November to 5 December 2025 (OJ C, C/2026/2102, 29.4.2026, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/C/2026/2102/oj). 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.8.2026) The EU applies a risk-based approach to hunting trophy imports under the EU Wildlife Trade Regulations1. Trophies imported for non-commercial purposes are generally treated as personal effects.

However, stricter requirements apply to the first introduction into the EU of trophies from 12 Annex B-listed species included in Annex XIII to the Implementing Regulation (EC) No 865/20062. These species require a non-detriment finding by the scientific authority of the Member State of destination. Applying the same requirements to all Annex B species would not reflect different conservation situations and risks.

Where import permits are not required, imports remain subject to the EU Wildlife Trade Regulations and the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora framework. The Commission, supported by the Scientific Review Group (SRG)3, monitors conservation status and trade patterns based on scientific information.

The revised EU Action Plan against Wildlife Trafficking4 lays down measures for increased scrutiny for additional Annex B species. The SRG is currently examining available evidence, but no decision has been taken yet. The Commission and the scientific authorities of the Member States assess scientific and trade information for possible amendments to Annex XIII.

Any future inclusion of species would rely on evidence concerning conservation status, trade sustainability and illegal trade risks, in line with the precautionary, risk- and science-based approach of the EU Wildlife Trade Regulations.
